title: Forgiveness: pardon and overlook
hook: a father swears to cut off the relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him a question

segments.voice: Yesterday, sidq, and your line: with the truthful. Did you reach out to one honest friend? Today, what to do when someone close has not been truthful at all. Day one thousand three hundred ten.

Abu Bakr had been supporting a poor relative, a man named Mistah. Then a false accusation spread through Medina about Abu Bakr's own daughter, 'A'ishah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. And Mistah was one of those who repeated it. When the Qur'an cleared her name, Abu Bakr made an oath, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: by Allah, I will never spend anything on Mistah again. On its face, a fair oath. A verse came down about it anyway.
screen: `ABU BAKR SUPPORTED MISTAH.` → `MISTAH SPREAD THE SLANDER.` → `AN OATH: NEVER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The verse is in surah al-Nur. It speaks to people of means who swear off giving to their relatives and the needy. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." Two verbs: forgive, and show indulgence. In Arabic, wal-ya'fu wal-yasfahu. Pardon, and overlook. 'Afw is letting go of what you're owed: the debt, the punishment, the right to get even. Overlooking goes one step further: not raising it again, not keeping it ready for the next argument. And then the question. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? The verse doesn't argue that Mistah deserved help. It doesn't say the slander was small. It asks Abu Bakr about himself. Do you want to be forgiven? Here's what he said, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me. And he went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Notice the order. The wrong was named first. 'A'ishah's innocence was declared in the Qur'an itself. Pardon came after the truth, not instead of it. The hadith on humility from a few days ago, in Sahih Muslim, has a line for this too, in paraphrase: no servant pardons except that Allah increases him in honor. In that hadith's terms, pardon costs no honor. So 'afw isn't pretending. It's choosing, with the wrong fully seen, to let the debt go, and then to stop bringing it up.
screen: `AL-NUR: FORGIVE AND SHOW INDULGENCE.` · `PARDON, THEN OVERLOOK.` · `DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `THE TRUTH FIRST, THEN PARDON.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who owes you something: an apology, money, a fairer word. Not the deepest wound you carry. Something you can hold. Name the wrong to yourself, plainly. Don't shrink it. Then hear the verse's question, turned toward you: is there anything you hope to be forgiven for? Stay with that for a few breaths. If you're ready, let one piece of the debt go. Maybe not all of it. If you pray, you can recite the verse's last words in your heart: Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. The bell holds the time.
'Afw. Pardon: letting go of what you're owed, with the wrong fully seen, and then overlooking it, not bringing it up again. Today's word.
Your line: pardon and overlook. Today, pardon one person for one thing, and then don't mention it again. Tomorrow, gentleness in all things. Day one thousand three hundred ten.

howItsDone: Islamic teaching on pardon draws on Qur'an 24:22 and the story of Abu Bakr resuming his support for Mistah, and on the hadith that Allah increases in honor a servant who pardons.

myth: the verse says the slander was a small thing
it doesn't. 'A'ishah's innocence was declared first; pardon came after the truth.
Abu Bakr returned to supporting Mistah
yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me, he said, and resumed it (Bukhari).
overlooking means you never admit you were wronged
the wrong is named and seen; overlooking means not bringing it up again.

fork.setup: you're Abu Bakr. you've sworn never to support Mistah again. a verse asks: don't you want Allah to forgive you? what do you do?
options: keep the oath; he earned it.
say yes, and go back to supporting him.
support him, but remind him of it often.
fork.reveal: he said: yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me, and restored Mistah's support (Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: pardon, letting go of what is owed.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving means acting like it never happened.
what it means: pardoning what you're owed with the wrong fully seen, then overlooking it, not raising it again.
what a scholar hears: al-Nur 24:22 pairs 'afw with safh; Bukhari 4750 ties the verse to Abu Bakr and Mistah after the accusation against 'A'ishah.

Editor: 'It sounds fair' changed to 'On its face, a fair oath' (no telling the listener how it sounds to them); the Muslim 2588 paraphrase now follows its wording (no one pardons except that Allah increases him in honor); cut 'Abu Bakr lost nothing by it', which no cited text says.
